sentences.text: The appeal is by the claimants seeking for enhancement of compensation.

3. The version of the appellants as could be perceived by the material available on record is that the deceased Shaik Afzal Pasha (herein after be referred to as deceased for brevity) was working as driver for a Tempo vehicle which belongs to Pw.2.
The deceased met with a road traffic accident on 18.03.2012 and succumbed to injuries.
The appellants claimed compensation of Rs.23,00,000/- in total.
However, the Tribunal through the impugned order has awarded a sum of Rs.11,00,000/- as compensation.

sentences.text: On this day learned counsel for the appellants attacked the impugned order by stating that though the appellants produced Ex.P9 - Salary Certificate and established its genuineness through the evidence of PW.2, NC: 2023:KHC:45312 the tribunal failed to consider the income of the deceased as put forth through the said evidence which is unjustifiable.
Learned counsel thereby seeks to take the amount mentioned in Ex.P9 as the salary of the deceased and thereby to revisit the calculation of compensation.

5. Opposing the said submission, learned counsel appearing for respondent No.2 submits that neither the GST registration certificates nor the income tax returns regarding Pw.2 were filed by the appellants.

Learned counsel also submits that even Ex.P9 was not issued over a letter head and thus the Tribunal had rightly set aside the said evidence and thereby arrived at a just conclusion with regard to the award of compensation.
6. The evidence of PW.2 is that he is owning Tempos since 10 years and usually he operate tempos by employing drivers.
In the year 2010 he purchased a Tempo medium goods vehicle bearing registration No.KA- 43-1401 for which he employed the deceased.
He stated that he paid salary of Rs.9,000/- p.m. besides batta of NC: 2023:KHC:45312 Rs.100/- per day for a period of 25-26 days a month.
He also stated that he issued Ex.P9 - Salary certificate and it bears his signature.

When the order of the Tribunal is gone through this Court finds that the Tribunal gave a finding to the effect that except the oral testimony of PW.2 and Ex.P9 there are no other records which are produced with regard to the income of the deceased.
The Tribunal also held that PW.2 has not produced the account extract or cash paid vouchers or receipts maintained by him with regard to salary and allowances of the deceased.

However, when the owner of the deceased himself appeared before Court and gave evidence with regard to the salary he was paying to the deceased and also issued a certificate which is brought on record by the appellants, this Court does not understand as to why credence could not be given to the said evidence oral and documentary.
Only because the relevant vouchers are not produced, the testimony of the witness cannot be thrown out.
As per the contents of the Ex.P9 and the evidence of PW.2, the deceased was being paid Rs.9,000/- p.m. salary besides batta of Rs.100/- per NC: 2023:KHC:45312 day for a period of 25-26 days a month.
Therefore, the salary of the deceased as per the evidence produced comes to Rs.11,500/- p.m.
The annual income of the deceased thus comes to Rs.1,38,000/- (Rs.11,500/- X 12).
If 30% is added towards future prospects, as added by the tribunal, the same comes to Rs.1,79,400/- (Rs.1,38,000 + Rs.41,400).
The dependents are admittedly 6 in number.

Therefore, if 1/4th of the income is deducted towards the personal and living expenses which the deceased would have incurred for himself had he been alive, the contribution of the deceased towards the appellants comes to Rs.1,34,550/- (Rs.1,79,400 - Rs.44,850).
On applying the appropriate multiplier i.e., 15 loss of dependency comes to Rs.20,18,250/-.
7. The Tribunal has awarded a sum of Rs.10,53,000/- towards loss of dependency.
In light of the aforementioned discussions the said amount is enhanced by Rs.9,65,250/-.
This Court does not find any other grounds to interfere with the impugned order.
